⟨η​Gt,Xt−Xt+1⟩F≤η22​λ​‖Gt‖∗2+λ2​‖Xt−Xt+1‖2.\langle\eta G_{t},X_{t}-X_{t+1}\rangle_{F}\leq\frac{\eta^{2}}{2\lambda}\|G_{t}\|_{*}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|X_{t}-X_{t+1}\|^{2}.

Then, since ψt\psi_{t} is λ\lambda-strongly convex w.r.t. ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|, it follows that

Bψt​(Xt+1,Xt)≥λ2​‖Xt−Xt+1‖2.B_{\psi_{t}}(X_{t+1};X_{t})\geq\frac{\lambda}{2}\|X_{t}-X_{t+1}\|^{2}.

⟨η​Gt,Xt−Xt+1⟩F−Bψt​(Xt+1,Xt)≤η22​λ​‖Gt‖∗2.\langle\eta G_{t},X_{t}-X_{t+1}\rangle_{F}-B_{\psi_{t}}(X_{t+1};X_{t})\leq\frac{\eta^{2}}{2\lambda}\|G_{t}\|_{*}^{2}.

Thus, the bound for η​⟨Gt,Xt−U⟩F\eta\langle G_{t},X_{t}-U\rangle_{F} simplifies to

η​⟨Gt,Xt−U⟩F≤Bψt​(U,Xt)−Bψt​(U,Xt+1)+η22​λ​‖Gt‖∗2.\eta\langle G_{t},X_{t}-U\rangle_{F}\leq B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t})-B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t+1})+\frac{\eta^{2}}{2\lambda}\|G_{t}\|_{*}^{2}.

This completes the proof of the one-step bound. ∎

Lemma 3 (Young’s Inequality for Matrices).

Let ℝm×n\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} be equipped with the Frobenius inner product. Let ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| be a norm on ℝm×n\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with its dual norm ∥⋅∥∗\|\cdot\|_{*} defined by

‖Y‖∗=sup‖X‖≤1|⟨X,Y⟩F|.\|Y\|_{*}=\sup_{\|X\|\leq 1}|\langle X,Y\rangle_{F}|.

Then for any A,B∈ℝm×nA,B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and scalar λ>0\lambda>0,

⟨A,B⟩F≤12​λ​‖A‖∗2+λ2​‖B‖2.\langle A,B\rangle_{F}\leq\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|A\|_{*}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|B\|^{2}.
Proof.

By the definition of the dual norm, we have

⟨A,B⟩F≤‖A‖∗⋅‖B‖.\langle A,B\rangle_{F}\leq\|A\|_{*}\cdot\|B\|.

To bound the product ‖A‖∗​‖B‖\|A\|_{*}\|B\|, consider the non-negative quadratic

(λ​‖B‖−‖A‖∗λ)2≥0.\left(\sqrt{\lambda}\|B\|-\frac{\|A\|_{*}}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\right)^{2}\geq 0.

Expanding the square yields

λ​‖B‖2−2​‖A‖∗​‖B‖+‖A‖∗2λ≥0.\lambda\|B\|^{2}-2\|A\|_{*}\|B\|+\frac{\|A\|_{*}^{2}}{\lambda}\geq 0.

Rearranging terms, we get

‖A‖∗​‖B‖≤12​λ​‖A‖∗2+λ2​‖B‖2.\|A\|_{*}\|B\|\leq\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|A\|_{*}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|B\|^{2}.

∎

Next, building on the one-step regret bound, we derive the final regret bound.

Proof.

Dividing the one-step bound by η\eta and summing over t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T gives

∑t=1T(ft​(Xt)−ft​(U))≤1η​∑t=1T(Bψt​(U,Xt)−Bψt​(U,Xt+1))+η2​λ​∑t=1T‖Gt‖∗2.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(X_{t})-f_{t}(U)\big)\leq\frac{1}{\eta}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big(B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t})-B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t+1})\Big)+\frac{\eta}{2\lambda}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|G_{t}\|_{*}^{2}.

We first rearrange the sum of Bregman divergences as

∑t=1T(Bψt​(U,Xt)−Bψt​(U,Xt+1))\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t})-B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t+1})\big) =Bψ1​(U,X1)−BψT​(U,XT+1)\displaystyle=B_{\psi_{1}}(U;X_{1})-B_{\psi_{T}}(U;X_{T+1})
+∑t=2TBψt(U;Xt)−∑t=1T−1Bψt(U;Xt+1).\displaystyle+\sum_{t=2}^{T}B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t+1}).

Re-indexing the first sum on the right-hand side by t↦t+1t\mapsto t+1, we obtain

∑t=2TBψt​(U,Xt)−∑t=1T−1Bψt​(U,Xt+1)=∑t=1T−1(Bψt+1​(U,Xt+1)−Bψt​(U,Xt+1)).\sum_{t=2}^{T}B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t+1})=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\Big(B_{\psi_{t+1}}(U;X_{t+1})-B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t+1})\Big).

Therefore,

∑t=1T(ft​(Xt)−ft​(U))\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(X_{t})-f_{t}(U)\big) ≤Bψ1​(U,X1)η−BψT​(U,XT+1)η\displaystyle\leq\frac{B_{\psi_{1}}(U;X_{1})}{\eta}-\frac{B_{\psi_{T}}(U;X_{T+1})}{\eta}
+1η∑t=1T−1(Bψt+1(U;Xt+1)−Bψt(U;Xt+1))+η2​λ∑t=1T∥Gt∥∗2.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{\eta}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\Big(B_{\psi_{t+1}}(U;X_{t+1})-B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t+1})\Big)+\frac{\eta}{2\lambda}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|G_{t}\|_{*}^{2}.

Since BψT​(U,XT+1)≥0B_{\psi_{T}}(U;X_{T+1})\geq 0, the negative term −BψT(U;XT+1)/η-B_{\psi_{T}}(U;X_{T+1})/{\eta} can be dropped to obtain the following regret bound

∑t=1T(ft​(Xt)−ft​(U))\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f_{t}(X_{t})-f_{t}(U)\big) ≤Bψ1​(U,X1)η+1η​∑t=1T−1(Bψt+1​(U,Xt+1)−Bψt​(U,Xt+1))\displaystyle\leq\frac{B_{\psi_{1}}(U;X_{1})}{\eta}+\frac{1}{\eta}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\Big(B_{\psi_{t+1}}(U;X_{t+1})-B_{\psi_{t}}(U;X_{t+1})\Big)
+η2​λ∑t=1T∥Gt∥∗2.\displaystyle+\frac{\eta}{2\lambda}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|G_{t}\|_{*}^{2}.

Since the above bound holds for every U∈𝒳U\in\mathcal{X}, we take U=X⋆∈arg​minX∈𝒳∑t=1Tft(X)U=X^{\star}\in\argmin_{X\in\mathcal{X}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(X), which yields the stated regret bound in Corollary 1. This completes the proof. ∎

Appendix C Proof of the Compact Form of the Bregman Matrix Divergence

Proposition 1.

Let ψtHt​(X)=12​Tr⁡(X⊤​Ht​X)\psi_{t}^{H_{t}}(X)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(X^{\top}H_{t}X) with Ht∈ℝm×mH_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} symmetric and positive definite. Then, for any two matrices X,Y∈ℝm×nX,Y\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, the Bregman matrix divergence induced by ψtHt\psi_{t}^{H_{t}} admits the compact form

BψtHt​(X,Y)=12​‖X−Y‖Ht2=12​Tr⁡((X−Y)⊤​Ht​(X−Y)).B_{\psi_{t}^{H_{t}}}(X;Y)=\frac{1}{2}\|X-Y\|_{H_{t}}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}((X-Y)^{\top}H_{t}(X-Y)).
Proof.

We start from the trace-based expression of the Bregman matrix divergence induced by ψtHt\psi_{t}^{H_{t}}

BψtHt​(X,Y)=12​Tr⁡(X⊤​Ht​X)−12​Tr⁡(Y⊤​Ht​Y)−Tr⁡(Y⊤​Ht​(X−Y)).B_{\psi_{t}^{H_{t}}}(X;Y)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(X^{\top}H_{t}X)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(Y^{\top}H_{t}Y)-\operatorname{Tr}\big(Y^{\top}H_{t}(X-Y)\big).

Expanding the last term using linearity of the trace gives

−Tr⁡(Y⊤​Ht​(X−Y))=−Tr⁡(Y⊤​Ht​X)+Tr⁡(Y⊤​Ht​Y).-\operatorname{Tr}\big(Y^{\top}H_{t}(X-Y)\big)=-\operatorname{Tr}(Y^{\top}H_{t}X)+\operatorname{Tr}(Y^{\top}H_{t}Y).

Substituting back and combining terms into a single trace, we obtain

BψtHt​(X,Y)\displaystyle B_{\psi_{t}^{H_{t}}}(X;Y) =12​Tr⁡(X⊤​Ht​X)−12​Tr⁡(Y⊤​Ht​Y)−Tr⁡(Y⊤​Ht​X)+Tr⁡(Y⊤​Ht​Y)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(X^{\top}H_{t}X)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(Y^{\top}H_{t}Y)-\operatorname{Tr}(Y^{\top}H_{t}X)+\operatorname{Tr}(Y^{\top}H_{t}Y)
=12​Tr⁡(X⊤​Ht​X−2​Y⊤​Ht​X+Y⊤​Ht​Y).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(X^{\top}H_{t}X-2Y^{\top}H_{t}X+Y^{\top}H_{t}Y).

Next, we separate the cross terms

X⊤​Ht​X−2​Y⊤​Ht​X+Y⊤​Ht​Y=X⊤​Ht​X−Y⊤​Ht​X−Y⊤​Ht​X+Y⊤​Ht​Y.X^{\top}H_{t}X-2Y^{\top}H_{t}X+Y^{\top}H_{t}Y=X^{\top}H_{t}X-Y^{\top}H_{t}X-Y^{\top}H_{t}X+Y^{\top}H_{t}Y.

Since HtH_{t} is symmetric, i.e., Ht⊤=HtH_{t}^{\top}=H_{t}, we have (X⊤​Ht​Y)⊤=Y⊤​Ht​X(X^{\top}H_{t}Y)^{\top}=Y^{\top}H_{t}X, which implies that Tr⁡(X⊤​Ht​Y)=Tr⁡(Y⊤​Ht​X)\operatorname{Tr}(X^{\top}H_{t}Y)=\operatorname{Tr}(Y^{\top}H_{t}X). Using this, the expression can be rewritten as

X⊤​Ht​X−X⊤​Ht​Y−Y⊤​Ht​X+Y⊤​Ht​Y.X^{\top}H_{t}X-X^{\top}H_{t}Y-Y^{\top}H_{t}X+Y^{\top}H_{t}Y.

Recognizing this as the expansion of a quadratic form, we have

(X−Y)⊤​Ht​(X−Y)=X⊤​Ht​X−X⊤​Ht​Y−Y⊤​Ht​X+Y⊤​Ht​Y.(X-Y)^{\top}H_{t}(X-Y)=X^{\top}H_{t}X-X^{\top}H_{t}Y-Y^{\top}H_{t}X+Y^{\top}H_{t}Y.

Hence,

X⊤​Ht​X−2​Y⊤​Ht​X+Y⊤​Ht​Y=(X−Y)⊤​Ht​(X−Y),X^{\top}H_{t}X-2Y^{\top}H_{t}X+Y^{\top}H_{t}Y=(X-Y)^{\top}H_{t}(X-Y),

and the Bregman matrix divergence can be expressed in compact quadratic form as

BψtHt​(X,Y)=12​Tr⁡((X−Y)⊤​Ht​(X−Y))=12​‖X−Y‖Ht2.B_{\psi_{t}^{H_{t}}}(X;Y)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}((X-Y)^{\top}H_{t}(X-Y))=\frac{1}{2}\|X-Y\|_{H_{t}}^{2}.

This completes the proof. ∎

Appendix D Derivation of the Dual Norm of the HtH_{t}-induced Matrix Norm

Proposition 2.

Let Ht∈ℝm×mH_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} be symmetric and positive definite. For any X∈ℝm×nX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, the HtH_{t}-induced matrix norm is ‖X‖Ht=⟨X,Ht​X⟩F\|X\|_{H_{t}}=\sqrt{\langle X,H_{t}X\rangle_{F}} , then for any G∈ℝm×nG\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, the corresponding dual norm is given by

‖G‖Ht∗=supX≠0⟨G,X⟩F‖X‖Ht=‖G‖Ht−1=Tr⁡(G⊤​Ht−1​G).\|G\|_{H_{t}}^{*}=\sup_{X\neq 0}\frac{\langle G,X\rangle_{F}}{\|X\|_{H_{t}}}=\|G\|_{H_{t}^{-1}}=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(G^{\top}H_{t}^{-1}G)}.

Equivalently, the squared dual norm is

‖G‖Ht∗2=‖G‖Ht−12=Tr⁡(G⊤​Ht−1​G).\|G\|_{H_{t}}^{*2}=\|G\|_{H_{t}^{-1}}^{2}=\operatorname{Tr}(G^{\top}H_{t}^{-1}G).
Proof.

By definition, the dual norm with respect to the Frobenius inner product is

‖G‖Ht∗=supX≠0⟨G,X⟩F‖X‖Ht.\|G\|_{H_{t}}^{*}=\sup_{X\neq 0}\frac{\langle G,X\rangle_{F}}{\|X\|_{H_{t}}}.

To simplify the supremum, consider the matrix square root of HtH_{t}, denoted Ht1/2H_{t}^{1/2}, which satisfies Ht=Ht1/2​Ht1/2H_{t}=H_{t}^{1/2}H_{t}^{1/2}. Defining Y=Ht1/2​XY=H_{t}^{1/2}X, we can invert this relation as X=Ht−1/2YX=H_{t}^{-1/2}Y, where Ht−1/2=(Ht1/2)−1.H_{t}^{-1/2}=(H_{t}^{1/2})^{-1}. This is well-defined since Ht1/2H_{t}^{1/2} is invertible (Ht≻0H_{t}\succ 0). Then

⟨G,X⟩F=⟨G,Ht−1/2Y⟩F=Tr(G⊤Ht−1/2Y).\langle G,X\rangle_{F}=\langle G,H_{t}^{-1/2}Y\rangle_{F}=\operatorname{Tr}\big(G^{\top}H_{t}^{-1/2}Y\big).

Since Ht−1/2H_{t}^{-1/2} is symmetric (being the inverse of a symmetric matrix), i.e., Ht−1/2=(Ht−1/2)⊤H_{t}^{-1/2}=(H_{t}^{-1/2})^{\top}, we can rewrite the trace as

Tr(G⊤Ht−1/2Y)=Tr((Ht−1/2G)⊤Y)=⟨Ht−1/2G,Y⟩F.\operatorname{Tr}\big(G^{\top}H_{t}^{-1/2}Y\big)=\operatorname{Tr}\big((H_{t}^{-1/2}G)^{\top}Y\big)=\langle H_{t}^{-1/2}G,Y\rangle_{F}.

Moreover, substituting X=Ht−1/2YX=H_{t}^{-1/2}Y into the HtH_{t}-induced norm gives

‖X‖Ht=⟨X,Ht​X⟩F=⟨Ht−1/2Y,Ht(Ht−1/2Y)⟩F.\|X\|_{H_{t}}=\sqrt{\langle X,H_{t}X\rangle_{F}}=\sqrt{\langle H_{t}^{-1/2}Y,H_{t}(H_{t}^{-1/2}Y)\rangle_{F}}.

Using HtHt−1/2=Ht1/2H_{t}H_{t}^{-1/2}=H_{t}^{1/2} (by the definition of the matrix square root), we have

⟨Ht−1/2Y,HtHt−1/2Y⟩F=⟨Ht−1/2Y,Ht1/2Y⟩F=Tr((Ht−1/2Y)⊤(Ht1/2Y)).\langle H_{t}^{-1/2}Y,H_{t}H_{t}^{-1/2}Y\rangle_{F}=\langle H_{t}^{-1/2}Y,H_{t}^{1/2}Y\rangle_{F}=\operatorname{Tr}\big((H_{t}^{-1/2}Y)^{\top}(H_{t}^{1/2}Y)\big).

Using the cyclic property of the trace, and the properties of Ht−1/2H_{t}^{-1/2}, we get

Tr((Ht−1/2Y)⊤(Ht1/2Y))=Tr(Y⊤(Ht−1/2Ht1/2)Y)=Tr(Y⊤Y)=⟨Y,Y⟩F=∥Y∥F2.\operatorname{Tr}\big((H_{t}^{-1/2}Y)^{\top}(H_{t}^{1/2}Y)\big)=\operatorname{Tr}\big(Y^{\top}(H_{t}^{-1/2}H_{t}^{1/2})Y\big)=\operatorname{Tr}(Y^{\top}Y)=\langle Y,Y\rangle_{F}=\|Y\|_{F}^{2}.

Thus, the HtH_{t}-induced norm of XX reduces exactly to the standard Frobenius norm of YY

‖X‖Ht=‖Y‖F.\|X\|_{H_{t}}=\|Y\|_{F}.

Hence, the dual norm becomes

‖G‖Ht∗=supY≠0⟨Ht−1/2G,Y⟩F‖Y‖F.\|G\|_{H_{t}}^{*}=\sup_{Y\neq 0}\frac{\langle H_{t}^{-1/2}G,Y\rangle_{F}}{\|Y\|_{F}}.

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, the supremum is attained when YY is a scalar multiple of Ht−1/2GH_{t}^{-1/2}G, which gives

‖G‖Ht∗=⟨Ht−1/2G,Ht−1/2G⟩F=Tr((Ht−1/2G)⊤(Ht−1/2G)).\|G\|_{H_{t}}^{*}=\sqrt{\langle H_{t}^{-1/2}G,H_{t}^{-1/2}G\rangle_{F}}=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}\big((H_{t}^{-1/2}G)^{\top}(H_{t}^{-1/2}G)\big)}.

By the symmetry of Ht−1/2H_{t}^{-1/2}, we have

Tr((Ht−1/2G)⊤(Ht−1/2G))=Tr(G⊤Ht−1/2Ht−1/2G).\operatorname{Tr}\big((H_{t}^{-1/2}G)^{\top}(H_{t}^{-1/2}G)\big)=\operatorname{Tr}\big(G^{\top}H_{t}^{-1/2}H_{t}^{-1/2}G\big).

Since Ht1/2H_{t}^{1/2} is the square root of HtH_{t}, we have

Ht=Ht1/2Ht1/2⟹Ht−1=Ht−1/2Ht−1/2.H_{t}=H_{t}^{1/2}H_{t}^{1/2}\quad\implies\quad H_{t}^{-1}=H_{t}^{-1/2}H_{t}^{-1/2}.

Therefore,

Tr((Ht−1/2G)⊤(Ht−1/2G))=Tr(G⊤Ht−1G)=⟨G,Ht−1G⟩F.\operatorname{Tr}\big((H_{t}^{-1/2}G)^{\top}(H_{t}^{-1/2}G)\big)=\operatorname{Tr}\big(G^{\top}H_{t}^{-1}G\big)=\langle G,H_{t}^{-1}G\rangle_{F}.

Hence, we obtain

‖G‖Ht∗=‖G‖Ht−1=Tr⁡(G⊤​Ht−1​G).\|G\|_{H_{t}}^{*}=\|G\|_{H_{t}^{-1}}=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}\big(G^{\top}H_{t}^{-1}G\big)}.

This completes the proof. Note that the derivation does not require HtH_{t} to be diagonal. ∎

Appendix E A Sufficient Condition for Fully Absorbing the Effect of the Stabilizer δ\delta

In this section, we derive a sufficient condition for fully offsetting the effect of the stabilizer δ\delta.

To completely remove the effect of the stabilizer δ\delta, it is sufficient to require

max1≤u≤T∥X∗−Xu∥:2,∞2mδ≤ 2BψTHT(X∗;XT+1).\,\max_{\mathclap{\scriptscriptstyle{1\leq u\leq T}}}\,\|X^{*}-X_{u}\|_{:2,\infty}^{2}\,m\delta\;\leq\;2B_{\psi_{T}^{H_{T}}}(X^{*};X_{T+1}).

Note that BψTHT​(X∗,XT+1)B_{\psi_{T}^{H_{T}}}(X^{*};X_{T+1}) still contains δ\delta. Expressing it in row-wise form and substituting sT,i=δ+∑t=1T∥Gt,i,:∥22,s_{T,i}=\delta+\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|G_{t,i,:}\|_{2}^{2}}, we have

BψTHT​(X∗,XT+1)\displaystyle B_{\psi_{T}^{H_{T}}}(X^{*}\!;X_{T+1}) =12∑i=1msT,i∥X∗i,:−XT+1,i,:∥22\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{m}s_{T,i}\|X^{*}_{i,:}-X_{T+1,i,:}\|_{2}^{2}
=12∑i=1m(δ+∑t=1T∥Gt,i,:∥22)∥Xi,:∗−XT+1,i,:∥22.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigg(\delta+\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|G_{t,i,:}\|_{2}^{2}}\bigg)\|X^{*}_{i,:}-X_{T+1,i,:}\|_{2}^{2}.

Thus, it is sufficient to require

max1≤u≤T∥X∗−Xu∥:2,∞2mδ≤∑i=1m∑t=1T∥Gt,i,:∥22∥X∗i,:−XT+1,i,:∥22.\max_{\scriptscriptstyle{1\leq u\leq T}}\!\|X^{*}-X_{u}\|_{:2,\infty}^{2}\,m\delta\;\leq\;\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|G_{t,i,:}\|_{2}^{2}}\,\|X^{*}_{i,:}-X_{T+1,i,:}\|_{2}^{2}.

Solving for δ\delta yields an explicit upper bound

δ≤∑i=1m∑t=1T∥Gt,i,:∥22∥Xi,:∗−XT+1,i,:∥22/(mmax1≤u≤T∥X∗−Xu∥:2,∞2).\delta\;\leq\;{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|G_{t,i,:}\|_{2}^{2}}\,\|X^{*}_{i,:}-X_{T+1,i,:}\|_{2}^{2}}\Big/{\Big(m\max_{1\leq u\leq T}\|X^{*}-X_{u}\|_{:2,\infty}^{2}}\Big).

By choosing δ\delta sufficiently small to satisfy this inequality, the additional contribution introduced by the stabilizer is fully absorbed by the negative terminal Bregman term, effectively eliminating its impact on the final regret bound.

Appendix F Column-AdaGrad Outperforms Entry-Wise AdaGrad: A Motivating Example

Recall that when applied to matrices, entry-wise AdaGrad treats an m×nm\times n matrix as a vector in ℝm​n\mathbb{R}^{mn} and applies independent per-coordinate step sizes. Its regret bound takes the form

Rvec​(T)≤2​𝒟∞​∑i=1m∑j=1n∑t=1TGt,i,j2,R_{\mathrm{vec}}(T)\leq\sqrt{2}\,\mathcal{D}_{\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}G_{t,i,j}^{2}},

where 𝒟∞=supX,Y∈𝒳‖X−Y‖∞\mathcal{D}_{\infty}=\sup_{X,Y\in\mathcal{X}}\|X-Y\|_{\infty} is the diameter of 𝒳\mathcal{X} under the entry-wise ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} norm.

We construct a scenario in which the data matrices are column-wise sparse, which leads to column-sparse gradients. We fix an integer K>0K>0 and set the horizon T=K​nT=Kn. For each column j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\dots,n\}, define the column-activated matrix D(j)=𝟏m​ej⊤D_{(j)}=\mathbf{1}_{m}e_{j}^{\top}, where eje_{j} is the jj-th standard basis vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and 𝟏m\mathbf{1}_{m} is the all-ones vector in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, so that D(j)D_{(j)} has ones in its jj-th column and zeros elsewhere. At each round t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T, a single column is activated cyclically: jt=((t−1)modn)+1j_{t}=((t-1)\bmod n)+1 and Dt=D(jt)D_{t}=D_{(j_{t})}. We consider the hinge loss

ft​(X)=max⁡{0, 1−yt​⟨X,Dt⟩F},f_{t}(X)=\max\big\{0,\;1-y_{t}\langle X,D_{t}\rangle_{F}\big\},

where yt=(−1)ty_{t}=(-1)^{t} is the label. We take the decision set to be the Frobenius norm ball 𝒳={X∈ℝm×n:‖X‖F≤B}\mathcal{X}=\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:\|X\|_{F}\leq B\} with radius B<1/mB<1/\sqrt{m}. Since ‖Dt‖F=m\|D_{t}\|_{F}=\sqrt{m}, this choice ensures that the margin is violated at every round, regardless of the player’s action: for all tt and all Xt∈𝒳X_{t}\in\mathcal{X},

yt​⟨Xt,Dt⟩F≤|⟨Xt,Dt⟩F|≤‖Xt‖F​‖Dt‖F≤B​m< 1.y_{t}\langle X_{t},D_{t}\rangle_{F}\;\leq\;\big|\langle X_{t},D_{t}\rangle_{F}\big|\;\leq\;\|X_{t}\|_{F}\|D_{t}\|_{F}\;\leq\;B\sqrt{m}\;<\;1.

Consequently, the subgradient of ftf_{t} at XtX_{t} is Gt=−yt​Dt=(−1)t+1​D(jt)G_{t}=-y_{t}D_{t}=(-1)^{t+1}D_{(j_{t})}, so that only the jtj_{t}-th column of GtG_{t} is nonzero, with all entries equal to ±1\pm 1. By construction, each column jj is activated exactly KK times, and a direct computation yields

∑i=1m∑j=1n∑t=1TGt,i,j2=mnK,∑j=1n∑t=1T∥Gt,:,j∥22=∑j=1n∑t=1T∑i=1mGt,i,j2=nm​K.\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}G_{t,i,j}^{2}}=mn\sqrt{K},\quad\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|G_{t,:,j}\|_{2}^{2}}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{m}G_{t,i,j}^{2}}=n\,\sqrt{mK}.

Moreover, the two diameter measures are 𝒟∞=supX,Y∈𝒳‖X−Y‖∞=2​B\mathcal{D}_{\infty}=\sup_{X,Y\in\mathcal{X}}\|X-Y\|_{\infty}=2B and 𝒟2:,∞=supX,Y∈𝒳∥X−Y∥2:,∞=2B\mathcal{D}_{2:,\infty}=\sup_{X,Y\in\mathcal{X}}\|X-Y\|_{2:,\infty}=2B. Both suprema are attained, for example, by taking X=B​E11X=BE_{11} and Y=−B​E11Y=-BE_{11}, where E11E_{11} denotes the matrix whose only nonzero entry is 11 at position (1,1)(1,1). Substituting the above quantities into the two respective regret bounds gives

Rvec​(T)≤2​2​B⋅m​n​K,Rcol​(T)≤2​2​B⋅n​m​K.R_{\mathrm{vec}}(T)\leq 2\sqrt{2}B\cdot mn\sqrt{K},\quad R_{\mathrm{col}}(T)\leq 2\sqrt{2}B\cdot n\,\sqrt{mK}.

The ratio of these two regret upper bounds is m\sqrt{m}, showing that Column-AdaGrad achieves a m\sqrt{m}-factor improvement in the regret bound over the entry-wise counterpart in this column-sparse setting.

Appendix G Variable-Depth Stacked MLP Training at a Smaller Learning Rate

Under exactly the same experimental configuration, we additionally reduce the learning rate from 0.010.01 to 0.0010.001 and evaluate both optimizers across different network depths. At 1515 layers, both methods exhibit substantially smaller loss fluctuations, while Row-wise Momentum still achieves a lower training loss than Adam. At 2525 layers, Row-wise Momentum remains able to train effectively, whereas Adam still completely fails to train. These results further indicate that, in this setting, row-wise scaling can support stable training at learning rates more than 10×10\times larger than those at which entry-wise scaling fails. This highlights a key advantage of row-wise adaptive scaling: its ability to maintain stable training at larger learning rates and greater network depths.
